questions.q: Which alkane can NOT be prepared by Kolbe electrolysis of an aqueous carboxylate salt?
questions.explain: Two alkyl radicals always couple, so the product has at least two carbons; even sodium acetate gives ethane. Methane can never be made this way.

questions.q: An aqueous solution of sodium butanoate is electrolysed. The hydrocarbon formed at the anode is:
questions.explain: The alkane has 2 × (carbons in the acid − 1) carbons: butanoate loses CO₂ to give a propyl radical, and two propyl radicals give hexane (C₆).

questions.q: During Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous sodium propanoate, which product is formed at the cathode?
questions.explain: Water is reduced at the cathode to H₂ and OH⁻, leaving NaOH in solution. Butane and CO₂ are both anode products, formed from oxidation of the carboxylate.

questions.q: A mixture of sodium acetate and sodium propanoate is electrolysed. The alkanes obtained are:
questions.explain: Methyl and ethyl radicals form at the anode, and all three combinations occur (CH₃–CH₃, CH₃–C₂H₅, C₂H₅–C₂H₅). That is why odd-carbon alkanes from this method come as mixtures.
